content.text: The text chiefly recounts Thomas Paine’s final years: his theism, criticism of Christianity, poverty, declining health, political persecution, disfranchisement, and defense against slanders about drunkenness and sexual misconduct. He lived in New Rochelle, then New York, later moved to Greenwich, and died there on June 8, 1809; he was buried on his New Rochelle farm. His bones were later exhumed by William Cobbett and taken to England. Appendices preserve accounts of Paine’s character, inventions, friendships, writings, and death. The text then shifts abruptly to Shire-horse breeding, export markets, prominent studs, and wartime prospects, before turning to Dutch East India Company administration in Jaffnapatam, Ceylon, including elephants, taxation, trade, rice, slavery, fortifications, courts, and public works.
